Molefe returns

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Did he resign? Did he retire? No-one knows ... but now Brian Molefe is back at Eskom as CEO

Unique Selling Point:
By allowing the return of Brian Molefe as CEO of Eskom, after he left six months ago "in the interests of good corporate governance", has the board of this public entity executed its fiduciary duties, adhered to principles of good governance and complied with all the labour laws of the country? We ask the experts.
Molefe's return comes after Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown blocked a pension payout of R30 million to Molefe, who only served as Eskom CEO (first acting, then permanent) for just less than 19 months. She sent the board back to the negotiating table with Molefe, and the board then decided to reverse all payouts to Molefe and reinstate him. Brown said it was a much better option than paying out R30 million - but is "the lesser of two evils" really the best solution for the country's crucial power utility?
Molefe himself said, when he resigned in the wake of the Public Protector's state capture report alleging wrongdoing on his part in relation to Gupta-linked companies, that he was leaving "because it is in the interests of Eskom and the public it serves". No investigation has as yet been done into the allegations against him but he returns, while his name has not yet been cleared.
We will interrogate Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown's assertion that Eskom will benefit from Molefe returning to the helm by compiling a timeline of Molefe's time at Eskom, punctuating the questionable dealings that took place in this period; and compiling a report card for Molefe, scoring his performance in areas such as electricity generation, finances, personnel and governance.
The Molefe decision has also highlighted cracks within the ANC, with the party criticising pres. Jacob Zuma's government for its actions, and Brown called to account to Luthuli House on Monday.

Summary:
In November, then Eskom CEO Brian Molefe announced that he decided to leave Eskom "in the interests of good corporate governance".
This after the former Public Protector Thuli Madonsela found, in her "State of Capture" report, that Molefe's ties to the Gupta family may have played a role in irregularities in dealings between Eskom and Gupta-linked companies.
Fast-forward six months and Molefe will be back at the helm of Eskom after his R30 million pension payout was blocked and the Eskom board then reversed its "decision to grant him early retirement". But when Molefe left in November, there was no mention of early retirement - something he was too young to qualify for anyway. Even Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown called his departure a "resignation" in a statement.
Now he will have to pay back some R7 million already paid out to him and he is set to complete his contract, which runs until September 2020.
Brown has said that steps must be taken to ensure that pension packages at state-owned companies are in line with cabinet approved remuneration standards - yet Molefe and the Eskom board continue as if nothing happened.
Brown has also reiterated her call for an investigation into allegations against Molefe, but says he is innocent until proven guilty and in the meantime he may return to run Eskom.
This while the position of Eskom CEO was advertised and candidates apparently already interviewed by a recruitment company.
The ANC has slammed the decision and called Brown to Luthuli House on Monday to account for it.
The DA wants to apply for an urgent interdict to prevent Molefe from returning to Eskom.

Press Release:


Six months ago Brian Molefe announced he was leaving Eskom. Since then, no investigation has been done into his friendship with the Guptas. Now he is back at the helm. Can the Eskom board justify this decision under South African law? Carte Blanche investigates his track record at Eskom, the reasons behind his departure and how he managed to return.

Script:


As hard as it is to imagine, the heat under South Africa’s political cauldron surged this week with outrage over state capture. The latest installment is the return of Brian Molefe as head of Eskom -- six months after he resigned amid allegations that he helped his and the president’s friends, the Guptas, in their dealings with Eskom.
When Molefe resigned he said it was in the interests of good governance and he would work to clear his name. In the meantime, he served as a member of parliament for the ANC and would have received R30 million in pension from Eskom. Even the ANC was outraged by his return to the state-owned company. ANC spokesman Zizi Kodwa.
ZIZI KODWA: We think that it undermines among others the public interest -- we can’t resolve issues as though we are tone deaf to the public cry about how government has become lackadaisical when it comes to corruption.
The country’s church leaders this week spoke out against state capture, saying that the government has lost its moral legitimacy. At Regina Mundi Church in Soweto, once a Struggle icon, the SA Council of Churches launched its Unburdening Panel, a facility for people to blow the whistle on corruption. Economist Iraj Abedian had high hopes for Molefe.
IRAJ ABEDIAN, INVESTMENT ANALYST: Here you have a man who steps down – and I praised him for that, to take accountability, to go out and clear his name. Far from clearing his name, he’s now confirmed by his own actions, the worst allegations that anybody has ever made against him. Neither did he clear his name, nor did he go out and challenge any of the issues legally. Far from it, he came back without any explanation.
Back at Eskom on Monday, Molefe was received with jubilation by staff. The DA has filed papers to ask the High Court in Pretoria for an urgent interdict to stop Molefe’s return.
BONGANI LINK: Eskom is our lifeblood. If they’re in trouble, so are we. Yet, over the years, members of the Carte Blanche team has stood at exactly this spot reflecting some or other crisis at Eskom. And here I am, back again.
The Eskom board decided to reinstate Molefe and Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown gave it the thumbs up – but they have been doing serious tapdancing to explain that he was not just reappointed without the job being advertised and the proper appointment processes followed. Labour lawyer Michael Bagraim spoke to us via Facetime from Cape Town.
MICHAEL BAGRAIM, LABOUR LAWYER: This is an industrial relations nightmare...it’s probably the worst I’ve seen in 35 years – I’ve been practising labour law for 35 years. Eskom in particular is very careful about the way in which it recruits and attempts to appoint people – staff go through a rigorous exercise each time they get appointed. You can’t just say this man used to work here, right we’re going to put him back into this job, we’ll parachute him in.
Abedian says even if there was nothing illegal about the matter, that’s just not good enough.
IRAJ ABEDIAN, INVESTMENT ANALYST: You can be within the law but be completely unethical. So what we have now at Eskom is a dereliction, meaning the collapse of ethics and corporate morality.
Eskom is a state-owned enterprise and is run with the public’s money. This, says the Institute of Directors of Southern Africa, means it has an even stricter duty to be transparent than other companies.
IRAJ ABEDIAN, INVESTMENT ANALYST: The growth of the economy, the perception of the economy and to some extent the perception of SA, links to how Eskom is perceived. There is a clear case at present for a board and its members who are derelict in terms of the fiduciary responsibilities of directors.
The King IV Report on Corporate Governance in South Africa is a set of principles and practices for good corporate governance -- and places effective and ethical leadership at the heart of this. The Eskom board is ultimately responsible for the finances and governance of Eskom.
IRAJ ABEDIAN, INVESTMENT ANALYST: Everybody knows that the board of Eskom is incompetent to manage a corner café, never mind an organisation like Eskom. And yet the minister is sitting doing nothing.
BONGANI BINGWA: What does this mean for the chairperson of the board? Dr Ben Ngubane?
MICHAEL BAGRAIM, labour lawyer: The chairperson unfortunately is the person who finally puts signature to paper. And that’s the person who’s going to have to explain in the cold, harsh light of a courtroom what actually has happened over here...it will go to court.
Eskom board spokesman Khulani Qoma said Molefe’s reinstatement was well-considered and prudent -- Molefe is a seasoned businessman who set Eskom on a sustainable future.
BONGANI LINK: Is Brian Molefe’s return good for Eskom? Well, there’s only one way to answer that question and that’s to ask, how well did he do the first time?
Molefe was acting and then permanent CEO from April 2015 to November 2016.
(TIMELINE) In September 2015: Eskom was given an R80-billion government bail-out. January 2016: Gupta-owned company Tegeta bought Optimum coal mine. February 2016: Treasury started investigating Eskom’s coal-supply contracts. August: Carte Blanche exposed gross overspending in the construction of hydro-power station Ingula. September: Two financial institutions discontinued loans as Moody’s threatened a downgrade.
Molefe had been hailed as Mr. Fix-it at the Public Investment Corporation and Transnet. At Eskom, Molefe is credited with bringing an end to loadshedding. Energy analyst Chris Yelland.
(PERFORMANCE REVIEW: MANAGEMENT) CHRIS YELLAND, Energy analyst: Eskom is not a one-band. Mr Molefe was the leader of a team and a whole organisation and something like 50 000 employees, so there’s a CEO and there’s a team of executives, senior management, middle management and I think his major achievement was to re-motivate his executive team to focus on the real issues, facing the organisation and to lift their morale. And I think that is a notable achievement in its own right.
(PERFORMANCE ON: POWER GENERATION) IRAJ ABEDIAN, Investment analyst: This façade of saviour does not stand scrutiny of the facts. What saved eskom from loadshedding was nothing other than the fact that economic growth collapsed. If today the economic growth revives to 2%, Eskom will go to blackout again. Nothing is saved. And this is not Mr Molefe’s fault. There is an energy policy problem here.
Eskom’s Standard and Poor’s credit rating is now just above junk status.
CHRIS YELLAND, Energy analyst: That is giving a message about financial sustainability, environment sustainability, operational sustainability, leadership, governance, etcetera. So the picture is not a pretty one ...
In November 2016 the Public Protector released the State of Capture report where she noted that allegations made about Molefe’s relationship with the Guptas were backed by evidence.
Molefe denied wrongdoing and said he wasn’t given a chance to explain why he spent so much time on the phone to the Guptas or in their fancy Joburg suburb Saxonwold. A week later, he told the nation he was leaving Eskom.
The wheels for Molefe’s return started turning when Brown blocked the payout of a pension package of R30 million to him. He earned R8-million a year -- nowhere near enough to justify a payout of that size.
Board chairman Ben Ngubane said the R30 million was compensation because they appointed Molefe permanently but then realised he should only have been given a five-year contract.
BEN NGUBANE: Our people in governance sat with him...recommended to the board...that was way back in 2015...that we buy ten years' pension for him to compensate for the gap that would be created in his pension when he retired in 10 years’ time.
When Molefe left, he simply said “I go now”. Brown said he resigned. Explaining his return, the Eskom Board said he had taken early retirement. But the law doesn’t fudge these things.
MICHAEL BAGRAIM, labour lawyer: It can’t be a retirement, he’s 51 years old and the pension fund rules are absolutely straight, honest, solid...you must be 55 to take early retirement...the receiver of revenue needs to know whether this is a severance package, because then there’s tax implications – whether it’s a gold handshake – has other types of tax implications...or whether it is actually retirement...they’re trying to dress it up as retirement, which would also be cheating the receiver.
The board told Brown that reinstating Molefe was the only way to avoid paying the R30 million.
MICHAEL BAGRAIM, labour lawyer: The only reinstatement that can happen is when a court reinstates you, a labour court, or the CCMA...the reinstatement means you get all your back pay from the date they last paid you. I would hate, today, to be sitting in the human resource office and facing a union negotiator. Can you imagine you’re in those shoes of a human resource executive, trying to explain away this precedent…
The ANC called Brown to headquarters at Luthuli House to explain herself.
ZIZI KODWA, ANC spokesperson: The minister was here this Monday, met with the national officials, the Top Six, to get the rationale behind such decision -- our position is that statement was reckless and insensitive. Our view still remains that decision must be reversed, must be rescinded.
BONGANI BINGWA: So are you saying she has committed to rescind the decision
ZIZI KODWA, ANC spokesperson: It’s a decision of the organisation we are deployees of the organisation -- they don’t have other options.
BONGANI LINK: As a member of cabinet, Minister Lynne Browne serves at the pleasure of the president but the ANC insists they are both deployees of the party and therefore must fulfil its agenda -- so who’s in charge?
Brown’s spokesman said that she is talking to president Jacob Zuma and deputy president Cyril Ramaphosa about how to resolve the Molefe issue.
BONGANI BINGWA: Does Brian Molefe face the real prospect of walking away from this at the end of the day with nothing?
MICHAEL BAGRAIM, LABOUR LAWYER: He certainly does and unfortunately it might not even have been his fault...it might be people outside who are using him as some sort of pawn – the litigation will follow...I believe that any court and particular the Labour Court will rule it out of order.
ZIZI KODWA, ANC spokesperson: Our view is that SOCs are quite important in the developmental agenda of the developmental state -- they can’t be run like family trust -- it can’t be run like spaza shops. Someone resigns tomorrow -- for some reason you come back with your clear conditions -- if you don’t reappoint me, I want R30-million -- it doesn’t work like that in any democracy.
BONGANI LINK: Given the very serious concerns raised by the Public Protector’s State of Capture report, specifically around Brian Molefe’s conduct, the question must be asked, whom does his redeployment really serve?


PROMOS
10 seconds
Out with tears and back in with song and dance. But can Eskom -- and the country -- survive the return of Brian Molefe?

15 seconds
Did he resign? Did he retire? The circumstances of Brian Molefe's departure from Eskom are unclear -- but he’s back as CEO. Can this be justified?
CHRIS YELLAND: I believe at the moment is a sorry picture of governance and unfortunately I don’t think the worst has hit us yet.

15 seconds
Can Eskom’s board justify the return of Brian Molefe under South African laws?
ZIZI KODWA: Someone resigns tomorrow -- for some reason you come back with conditions -- if you don’t reappoint me, I want R30-million -- it doesn’t work like that in any democracy.

And that’s the person who’s going to have to explain in the cold, harsh light of a courtroom what actually has happened over here...it will go to court. Eskom board spokesman Khulani Qoma said Molefe’s reinstatement was well-considered and prudent -- Molefe is a seasoned businessman who set Eskom on a sustainable future. BONGANI LINK: Is Brian Molefe’s return good for Eskom? Well, there’s only one way to answer that question and that’s to ask, how well did he do the first time? Molefe was acting and then permanent CEO from April 2015 to November 2016. (TIMELINE) In September 2015: Eskom was given an R80-billion government bail-out. January 2016: Gupta-owned company Tegeta bought Optimum coal mine. February 2016: Treasury started investigating Eskom’s coal-supply contracts. August: Carte Blanche exposed gross overspending in the construction of hydro-power station Ingula. September: Two financial institutions discontinued loans as Moody’s threatened a downgrade. Molefe had been hailed as Mr. Fix-it at the Public Investment Corporation and Transnet. At Eskom, Molefe is credited with bringing an end to loadshedding. Energy analyst Chris Yelland. (PERFORMANCE REVIEW: MANAGEMENT) CHRIS YELLAND, Energy analyst: Eskom is not a one-band. Mr Molefe was the leader of a team and a whole organisation and something like 50 000 employees, so there’s a CEO and there’s a team of executives, senior management, middle management and I think his major achievement was to re-motivate his executive team to focus on the real issues, facing the organisation and to lift their morale. And I think that is a notable achievement in its own right. (PERFORMANCE ON: POWER GENERATION) IRAJ ABEDIAN, Investment analyst: This façade of saviour does not stand scrutiny of the facts. What saved eskom from loadshedding was nothing other than the fact that economic growth collapsed. If today the economic growth revives to 2%, Eskom will go to blackout again. Nothing is saved. And this is not Mr Molefe’s fault. There is an energy policy problem here. Eskom’s Standard and Poor’s credit rating is now just above junk status. CHRIS YELLAND, Energy analyst: That is giving a message about financial sustainability, environment sustainability, operational sustainability, leadership, governance, etcetera. So the picture is not a pretty one ... In November 2016 the Public Protector released the State of Capture report where she noted that allegations made about Molefe’s relationship with the Guptas were backed by evidence. Molefe denied wrongdoing and said he wasn’t given a chance to explain why he spent so much time on the phone to the Guptas or in their fancy Joburg suburb Saxonwold. A week later, he told the nation he was leaving Eskom. The wheels for Molefe’s return started turning when Brown blocked the payout of a pension package of R30 million to him. He earned R8-million a year -- nowhere near enough to justify a payout of that size. Board chairman Ben Ngubane said the R30 million was compensation because they appointed Molefe permanently but then realised he should only have been given a five-year contract. BEN NGUBANE: Our people in governance sat with him...recommended to the board...that was way back in 2015...that we buy ten years' pension for him to compensate for the gap that would be created in his pension when he retired in 10 years’ time. When Molefe left, he simply said “I go now”. Brown said he resigned. Explaining his return, the Eskom Board said he had taken early retirement. But the law doesn’t fudge these things. MICHAEL BAGRAIM, labour lawyer: It can’t be a retirement, he’s 51 years old and the pension fund rules are absolutely straight, honest, solid...you must be 55 to take early retirement...the receiver of revenue needs to know whether this is a severance package, because then there’s tax implications – whether it’s a gold handshake – has other types of tax implications...or whether it is actually retirement...they’re trying to dress it up as retirement, which would also be cheating the receiver. The board told Brown that reinstating Molefe was the only way to avoid paying the R30 million. MICHAEL BAGRAIM, labour lawyer: The only reinstatement that can happen is when a court reinstates you, a labour court, or the CCMA...the reinstatement means you get all your back pay from the date they last paid you. I would hate, today, to be sitting in the human resource office and facing a union negotiator. Can you imagine you’re in those shoes of a human resource executive, trying to explain away this precedent… The ANC called Brown to headquarters at Luthuli House to explain herself. ZIZI KODWA, ANC spokesperson: The minister was here this Monday, met with the national officials, the Top Six, to get the rationale behind such decision -- our position is that statement was reckless and insensitive. Our view still remains that decision must be reversed, must be rescinded. BONGANI BINGWA: So are you saying she has committed to rescind the decision ZIZI KODWA, ANC spokesperson: It’s a decision of the organisation we are deployees of the organisation -- they don’t have other options. BONGANI LINK: As a member of cabinet, Minister Lynne Browne serves at the pleasure of the president but the ANC insists they are both deployees of the party and therefore must fulfil its agenda -- so who’s in charge? Brown’s spokesman said that she is talking to president Jacob Zuma and deputy president Cyril Ramaphosa about how to resolve the Molefe issue. BONGANI BINGWA: Does Brian Molefe face the real prospect of walking away from this at the end of the day with nothing? MICHAEL BAGRAIM, LABOUR LAWYER: He certainly does and unfortunately it might not even have been his fault...it might be people outside who are using him as some sort of pawn – the litigation will follow...I believe that any court and particular the Labour Court will rule it out of order. ZIZI KODWA, ANC spokesperson: Our view is that SOCs are quite important in the developmental agenda of the developmental state -- they can’t be run like family trust -- it can’t be run like spaza shops. Someone resigns tomorrow -- for some reason you come back with your clear conditions -- if you don’t reappoint me, I want R30-million -- it doesn’t work like that in any democracy. BONGANI LINK: Given the very serious concerns raised by the Public Protector’s State of Capture report, specifically around Brian Molefe’s conduct, the question must be asked, whom does his redeployment really serve? The circumstances of Brian Molefe's departure from Eskom are unclear -- but he’s back as CEO. Can this be justified? CHRIS YELLAND: I believe at the moment is a sorry picture of governance and unfortunately I don’t think the worst has hit us yet. 15 seconds Can Eskom’s board justify the return of Brian Molefe under South African laws? metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Did he resign? Did he retire? No-one knows ... but now Brian Molefe is back at Eskom as CEO
metadata.Unique Selling Point: By allowing the return of Brian Molefe as CEO of Eskom, after he left six months ago "in the interests of good corporate governance", has the board of this public entity executed its fiduciary duties, adhered to principles of good governance and complied with all the labour laws of the country? We ask the experts. Molefe's return comes after Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown blocked a pension payout of R30 million to Molefe, who only served as Eskom CEO (first acting, then permanent) for just less than 19 months. She sent the board back to the negotiating table with Molefe, and the board then decided to reverse all payouts to Molefe and reinstate him. Brown said it was a much better option than paying out R30 million - but is "the lesser of two evils" really the best solution for the country's crucial power utility? Molefe himself said, when he resigned in the wake of the Public Protector's state capture report alleging wrongdoing on his part in relation to Gupta-linked companies, that he was leaving "because it is in the interests of Eskom and the public it serves". No investigation has as yet been done into the allegations against him but he returns, while his name has not yet been cleared. We will interrogate Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown's assertion that Eskom will benefit from Molefe returning to the helm by compiling a timeline of Molefe's time at Eskom, punctuating the questionable dealings that took place in this period; and compiling a report card for Molefe, scoring his performance in areas such as electricity generation, finances, personnel and governance. The Molefe decision has also highlighted cracks within the ANC, with the party criticising pres. Jacob Zuma's government for its actions, and Brown called to account to Luthuli House on Monday.
metadata.Summary: In November, then Eskom CEO Brian Molefe announced that he decided to leave Eskom "in the interests of good corporate governance". This after the former Public Protector Thuli Madonsela found, in her "State of Capture" report, that Molefe's ties to the Gupta family may have played a role in irregularities in dealings between Eskom and Gupta-linked companies. Fast-forward six months and Molefe will be back at the helm of Eskom after his R30 million pension payout was blocked and the Eskom board then reversed its "decision to grant him early retirement". But when Molefe left in November, there was no mention of early retirement - something he was too young to qualify for anyway. Even Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown called his departure a "resignation" in a statement. Now he will have to pay back some R7 million already paid out to him and he is set to complete his contract, which runs until September 2020. Brown has said that steps must be taken to ensure that pension packages at state-owned companies are in line with cabinet approved remuneration standards - yet Molefe and the Eskom board continue as if nothing happened. Brown has also reiterated her call for an investigation into allegations against Molefe, but says he is innocent until proven guilty and in the meantime he may return to run Eskom. This while the position of Eskom CEO was advertised and candidates apparently already interviewed by a recruitment company. The ANC has slammed the decision and called Brown to Luthuli House on Monday to account for it. The DA wants to apply for an urgent interdict to prevent Molefe from returning to Eskom.
